content:
Asus ProArt PA27UCGE is a 27-inch 4K monitor that stands out in the fiercely competitive monitor market thanks to several unique features. First, it supports a high refresh rate of up to 160Hz, delivering exceptionally smooth visuals whether you're browsing the web, gaming, or editing videos. It also comes with an optional monitor hood to help reduce ambient light interference, and the built-in motorized colorimeter can automatically perform calibration on a schedule.

We previously reviewed Asus's 5K ProArt (review) and 6K ProArt monitors (review), and found both to be solid value-for-money third-party options for Mac users. So how does this 4K ProArt monitor perform? Watch our hands-on video review to find out.

The Asus ProArt monitor series has always focused on photo editing and video production, and this 27-inch 4K PA27UCGE is no exception. While it doesn't deliver the deep blacks of OLED, I found that this 600-nit IPS panel offers good contrast and stable brightness output, making it suitable for work in environments where lighting isn't fully controlled.

Video: Asus 4K 160Hz Monitor—Is It Worth Buying?

The PA27UCGE supports variable refresh rates up to 160Hz at 4K resolution. Beyond making text scrolling smoother, it's also well-suited for high-frame-rate video production and gaming. I tested it alongside my own 16-inch MacBook Pro (equipped with 120Hz ProMotion), and the matching refresh rates on both screens felt great. Even when connected to an M4 Mac mini alone, being able to use 120Hz, 144Hz, or even 160Hz made for a very comfortable experience.

Although I still prefer glossy monitors over matte ones, this screen uses an anti-glare, low-reflectivity "LuxPixel" coating that suppresses reflections while keeping text crisp and sharp, without the text blurring commonly seen on typical matte screens. To be clear, text is still affected to some degree, but among matte screens, this is the best performer I've seen besides Apple's nano-etch option.

The PA27UCGE also comes with an optional monitor hood to help block ambient light reflections. I found the process of attaching the hood somewhat annoying—the design and build feel a bit clumsy—but once installed, it does effectively prevent ambient light from hitting the screen surface.

macOS Scaling Settings

One of the drawbacks of using a 4K monitor with macOS is that it can't display at a perfect native 1:1 ratio at HiDPI 2880×1440, which is what many people want on a screen of this size. Like all 4K monitors on macOS, if you set the display to 2560×1440, the system first renders at a virtual canvas of 5120×2880, then applies fractional scaling down to a pixel-doubled 1440p "retina" HiDPI resolution. Although the result comes very close to a true 5K panel, because it's not a perfect 1:1 ratio, text sharpness takes a slight hit.

If you use the native pixel-doubled 1920×1080 resolution, you get a true 1:1 ratio with extremely sharp text, but at the cost of reduced workspace. For most people, sacrificing a bit of sharpness for more usable space is a reasonable trade-off, but it's worth keeping in mind. I used to be more sensitive to this issue when my eyes were better, but now that I'm older, I find it acceptable and no longer a major problem.

Calibration Measurement Results

The monitor has a built-in motorized colorimeter beneath the logo on the bottom bezel, allowing the ProArt 4K to calibrate itself without needing additional external calibration tools or software for more accurate colors. That said, I still prefer using an external tool like the Calibrite Display Pro HL for its greater flexibility.

Calibration can be performed via the OSD using the built-in motorized colorimeter, but if you want to see actual data, you'll need to install the Asus ProArt calibration tool. The limitation of the built-in colorimeter is its fixed position, but one of its biggest advantages is that it can run scheduled calibrations automatically when the monitor isn't in use. Since calibration can easily take 30 minutes or more, this is very convenient in the long run.

According to the included calibration report, this sample unit had a Delta-E sRGB average of 0.78 and a DCI-P3 average of 1.12—both excellent figures. This metric measures the difference between the original input colors and what's actually displayed on screen; the lower the number, the higher the color accuracy. In my experience, anything below 2 is considered good.

Asus claims the PA27UCGE offers 98% DCI-P3 color gamut coverage, making it well-suited for color grading and video editing in Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve. To verify Asus's claims, I tested using both the built-in colorimeter and my Calibrite Display Pro HL, paired with Calibrite Profiler software and Asus's ProArt calibration tool.

My measurements showed a DCI-P3 Delta E average of < 1.2, closely matching Asus's claimed figures. DCI-P3 color gamut coverage was also very accurate. When I edited and color-graded Canon Log 2 footage shot on my Canon R5 Mark II in Final Cut Pro, the colors were largely accurate.

More importantly, the monitor panel showed good color and brightness uniformity, with brightness deviation staying within < 5 in nearly all Calibrite Profiler tests. On the brightness front, the monitor is rated for a maximum of 600 nits, but in my testing it peaked at over 700 nits.

Design, Build, and Ergonomics

The ASUS ProArt 4K monitor follows the traditional Asus design language—same as the previous Asus ProArt 5K and 6K monitors—and isn't particularly outstanding in build quality. That's not to say Asus's build is poor; it's just that Apple has put a lot of effort into this area, so Apple's own displays are almost always manufactured to a higher standard.

Third-party monitor makers generally struggle to compete with Apple in this regard. Instead, third-party monitors typically offer better value at a more affordable price, using primarily plastic bodies that are easier to mass-produce, but with richer feature sets.

All this really boils down to: of course, I'd love for Asus's monitors to use unibody aluminum construction with smooth adjustment and balanced mechanisms, but the reality is that you won't find any third-party monitor manufacturer willing to go head-to-head with Apple on that front. Asus's approach is to deliver better value at lower cost, with higher refresh rates and more I/O options, among other things.

Ergonomics

In terms of ergonomics, the Asus ProArt 4K is well-equipped. The monitor supports +23 to -5 degrees of tilt adjustment, bidirectional 90-degree pivot, ±30 degrees of swivel, and 120mm of height adjustment. The smoothness and balance of the adjustments don't quite match the Apple Studio Display. Apple includes tilt adjustment even on the base Studio Display, with an upgrade to a tilt- and height-adjustable stand costing an extra $200, but it offers no rotation support at all.

My overall impression of the Asus PA27UCGE's design, build, and ergonomics is that it prioritizes function over form. Of course, I'd love it if its front bezel were as clean as the Studio Display's, with no logo and no buttons, but at an $800 price point, this Asus 4K monitor is unbeatable value.

Ports

Although Apple added Thunderbolt 5 and daisy-chaining to the new Studio Display, third-party monitors like the PA27UCGE offer a more comprehensive selection.

The USB 3.2 Gen 1 upstream port is the primary connection most Mac users will use to hook up a MacBook or Mac mini. For laptop users, this USB upstream port can deliver up to 96W of power—enough to fast-charge a 14-inch MacBook Pro at full speed. The PA27UCGE also comes with two HDMI 2.1 ports and a DisplayPort 1.4 connection, making it easy to hook up a PC, game console, or set-top box like an Apple TV.

  • Digital Inputs: 1 x DisplayPort v1.4, 2 x HDMI 2.1, 1 x DisplayPort over USB Type-C
  • USB Ports: 1 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 Upstream Type-C (data only), 1 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 Downstream Type-C, 2 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 Downstream Type-A
  • Audio: Headphone jack, Built-in speakers (2W x 2)

In addition to the built-in USB hub, the monitor also features auto-KVM functionality, making it easy to connect two computers simultaneously and share a single mouse and keyboard.

9to5Mac Verdict

The Asus ProArt Display PA27UCGE offers exceptional value at its price point. It delivers excellent DCI-P3 color support, making it ideal for photo and video editing, and its high refresh rate pairs perfectly with a ProMotion-equipped MacBook Pro.

The LuxPixel matte screen effectively suppresses reflections without seriously compromising text sharpness, and while the included monitor hood isn't particularly elegant in design, it does a decent job of blocking ambient light.

Let's not forget that this monitor offers a generous array of input options, including dual HDMI, DisplayPort, and USB-C, along with hub functionality and KVM support.

Like most third-party monitors on the market, the build quality still trails Apple's own displays, but that's true of nearly all third-party monitors. In compensation, it offers more comprehensive ergonomic adjustments.

Asus provides a 3-year warranty for ProArt monitors (including the PA27UCGE), extendable to a total of 5 years for free upon registration. When you think about it, most monitors on the market—including Apple's displays—only come with a 1-year warranty, so a 5-year warranty is extremely attractive.

Of course, this monitor isn't perfect, but at an $800 price point, the performance of this Asus ProArt 4K monitor is absolutely top-notch. For video editors or gamers seeking a high refresh rate, I can recommend it without reservation.
